messages.content: I want to develop visual anomaly detection that separates novel manufacturing defects from unseen illumination and camera shifts, using only defect-free training images. Under unseen benign shifts, the target is at least 90% defect recall at no more than a 5% image-level false-positive rate. Those targets need to hold separately for structural and texture defects, without anomalous calibration data.

The key distinction is between an actual manufacturing defect and a change in how a defect-free item appears because of illumination or the camera. The system needs to remain sensitive to novel defects while not treating unseen, benign shifts as defects. The ≥90% recall and ≤5% image-level false-positive rate are paired requirements under those shifts, and the requirement applies separately to structural and texture defects.
What does “novel” add here if the training images are all defect-free anyway?

It emphasizes that the target is not limited to recognizing defect examples encountered during training. Training uses only defect-free images, yet the detector is expected to identify manufacturing defects it has not been trained on as examples. That is different from learning to recognize a fixed collection of labeled defect appearances.
And the illumination or camera changes are not themselves supposed to count as anomalies?

Right. The specified illumination and camera shifts are benign: they can change an image without making the manufactured item defective. A defect-free image should not be called defective merely because it has one of those unseen shifts. At the same time, a real defect should remain detectable under such conditions.
Could the detector meet the recall target by flagging almost every shifted image?

No. Flagging many images could increase defect recall, but it would also produce false positives on defect-free images. The goal requires at least 90% defect recall while keeping the image-level false-positive rate at or below 5% under unseen benign shifts. Neither number is meant to be considered in isolation.
What exactly is image-level false-positive rate measuring in that statement?

It concerns defect-free images that are nevertheless flagged as anomalous. “Image-level” says the false-positive judgment is about whether an image is flagged, rather than, for example, counting individual marked regions. The limit is no more than 5% under the specified unseen benign shifts.
Does “image-level” also specify how defect recall must be measured?

The wording explicitly identifies the false-positive rate as image-level; it does not separately spell out the aggregation used for defect recall. What is clear is the required threshold—at least 90% defect recall—and that it must be met under unseen benign shifts while the image-level false-positive rate remains at or below 5%.
I also don't want a strong result on one defect type to hide a weak result on the other.

That is why the structural and texture requirements are separate. A combined recall figure would not, by itself, establish that both meet the target. The stated goal calls for the ≥90% defect-recall target, subject to the ≤5% image-level false-positive-rate limit, for structural defects and for texture defects separately.
Does that mean the system has to label each detected defect as structural or texture?

Not necessarily. Separate targets say how performance must hold for those two kinds of defects; they do not, on their own, require a particular output format or a separate classifier for each kind. The requirement is that neither category's performance be obscured by combining the results.
How should I read “without anomalous calibration data” alongside “only defect-free training images”?

They constrain different potential uses of defect examples. Training is based only on defect-free images, and calibration cannot rely on anomalous data either. In particular, the stated target cannot depend on using known defect examples to adjust a decision setting until the required recall and false-positive rate are obtained. The wording does not prescribe a specific alternative calibration method.
Does that ban observing defective images when checking whether the recall target was achieved?

No such ban on evaluation is stated. The restriction is on training images and anomalous calibration data. Assessing defect recall is a distinct matter from using anomalous examples to train or calibrate the detector; the goal does not provide a detailed evaluation procedure.
Is this mainly a demand for robustness to a different-looking image?

Robustness is part of it, but “different-looking” is too broad on its own. The detector should tolerate differences caused by unseen, benign illumination and camera shifts, without becoming insensitive to actual, novel manufacturing defects. The challenge is to distinguish those two reasons an image may differ from defect-free training images.
So a large visual change isn't automatically a defect, and a subtle one isn't automatically harmless?

Exactly. The goal is about whether there is a manufacturing defect, not about treating the magnitude of any visual difference as a verdict by itself. A benign shift must not consume more than the allowed image-level false-positive rate, while actual defects still have to meet the recall requirement. The node does not assume a particular visual magnitude for either kind of change.
Why name both illumination shifts and camera shifts instead of just saying there may be benign variation?

Naming both makes the intended distinction more specific: changes associated with illumination and changes associated with the camera are within the benign shifts the detector should handle, even when unseen. It does not specify their precise forms or say that one can stand in for the other. Both sit on the nondefect side of the distinction when they are benign.
Would an overall false-positive rate of 5% settle the structural-versus-texture question?

Not by itself. False positives concern images without defects; the separate structural and texture requirement chiefly prevents the defect-recall result for one category from masking the other. The ≤5% image-level false-positive-rate condition still has to accompany the required recall under unseen benign shifts, rather than being replaced by a recall figure averaged across defect categories.
Is there a specified model design or decision rule implied by these numbers?

No particular architecture, scoring rule, or way of setting a threshold is specified. The numbers describe the performance target, while the data restrictions describe what may be used for training and calibration. Choosing a method would be a separate question; these requirements alone do not establish that any method has achieved the target.
I want to be careful about what can be claimed before anything is tested.

Then it is best to keep the wording as a goal: develop a detector using only defect-free training images, with no anomalous calibration data, that distinguishes novel manufacturing defects from unseen benign illumination and camera shifts. Success would require ≥90% defect recall at ≤5% image-level false-positive rate under those shifts, separately for structural and texture defects. Those are requirements, not reported results.

For the proposed approach, call it ShiftGuard. It would learn registration-equivariant structural embeddings and relighting-invariant texture embeddings from augmented normal images, then calibrate separate 95th-percentile image-level thresholds. How does that connect to the detection goal?

ShiftGuard separates two kinds of representation. Its structural embeddings are intended to behave predictably when an image’s registration changes; its texture embeddings are intended to remain stable under relighting. Both are learned from augmented normal images, so the proposal does not depend on defect examples for learning those representations. The separate image-level thresholds keep the structural and texture scoring paths distinct. This describes an approach to the goal, not evidence that it already meets the recall or false-positive targets under unseen benign shifts.
Can you unpack “registration-equivariant”? Is that just another way of saying it ignores camera shifts?

Not quite. Equivariance means that when the input undergoes a relevant registration change, the structural representation changes in a corresponding, predictable way. Invariance would mean the representation stays the same. The proposed structural embedding is registration-equivariant, not simply indifferent to registration. That distinction matters because structural information can have a spatial arrangement that should remain interpretable when an image is re-registered.
And “relighting-invariant” means the texture embedding should not react to illumination changes?

It means the texture embedding is intended to stay stable under relighting, so an illumination change alone is less likely to look like a texture defect. It does not mean every possible lighting change is guaranteed to have no effect, or that the embedding should ignore actual texture defects. The proposal names the desired behavior, but its success under unseen shifts would still need to be assessed.
Why use different properties for structural and texture embeddings?

They address different ways benign image changes could interfere with defect detection. For structural information, predictable behavior under registration changes is the proposed property. For texture information, stability under relighting is the proposed property. Keeping those aims distinct is consistent with requiring performance to hold separately for structural and texture defects; it does not assume that a single representation handles both in the same way.
Does learning from augmented normal images mean ShiftGuard is trained with examples of camera and illumination changes?

The proposal specifies augmented normal images as its learning input, but does not give an augmentation recipe or enumerate which changes the augmentations contain. It is fair to say that augmentation is part of how ShiftGuard would learn the proposed embedding properties. It would go beyond the proposal to claim that the augmented images cover particular unseen shifts or that augmentation alone ensures robustness to them.
Would those augmented images still count as defect-free training images?

Yes, as described, the learning input is augmented normal images rather than anomalous examples. The intended training basis remains defect-free images. The proposal does not add defect examples for either the structural or texture embedding.
What does the 95th-percentile threshold do at the image level?

For an image-level score, a 95th-percentile threshold marks the upper end of the scores used for calibration: roughly the highest-scoring 5% lie above that percentile, subject to how the percentile and threshold comparisons are defined. ShiftGuard proposes separate thresholds, one associated with structural scoring and one with texture scoring. The proposal does not specify the score calculations or the exact calibration procedure.
Is setting each threshold at the 95th percentile enough to establish the ≤5% image-level false-positive rate?

No. A percentile describes the calibration scores on which it is set; it does not guarantee the same false-positive rate on unseen benign illumination or camera shifts. The observed rate could differ when the conditions change. The 95th-percentile choice is related to a nominal 5% upper tail, but the goal’s ≤5% image-level false-positive rate under unseen benign shifts remains a performance requirement to check, not an automatic consequence.
If there are two separate thresholds, can I treat either threshold being exceeded as the final image-level alert and still assume 5%?

The proposal does not specify how the two threshold results become a final alert. If an alert were issued whenever either threshold was exceeded, a 5% upper tail for each score individually would not, by itself, imply a 5% upper tail for that combined rule. The two sets of flagged images need not be identical. So the separate 95th-percentile thresholds should not be mistaken for a demonstrated ≤5% false-positive rate for an unspecified combined decision.
Could the two branches instead be thought of as serving the separate structural and texture targets?

That is the natural connection in the proposal: structural and texture embeddings, with separate image-level thresholds, give each defect type its own path for assessment. It still does not establish that either path reaches ≥90% defect recall, or that its image-level false-positive rate stays at ≤5% under unseen benign shifts. Those remain the stated targets for each defect category.
Does the proposal say how an image gets a structural score or a texture score?

No. It specifies the kinds of embeddings to learn and that separate 95th-percentile image-level thresholds are calibrated, but it does not specify a scoring formula. We can discuss what an image-level threshold means without assuming a particular distance measure, aggregation method, or comparison against normal images.
Nor does “registration-equivariant” tell us that ShiftGuard actually performs registration first, right?

Right. Registration-equivariant describes a desired relationship between changes in image registration and changes in the structural embedding. It does not, on its own, prescribe a registration step or a particular registration algorithm.
Does calibrating thresholds introduce anomalous calibration data?

Not as proposed. ShiftGuard is described as learning from augmented normal images, and the goal rules out anomalous calibration data. Separate 95th-percentile image-level thresholds can be framed in terms of normal-image scores without introducing defect examples. The proposal does not specify a separate calibration dataset or its construction, so those details should not be assumed.
I don't want the word “invariant” to imply that texture defects get erased along with relighting differences.

That would be too strong an inference. The proposed invariance concerns relighting, a benign source of variation; the detection goal still requires sensitivity to novel texture defects. Whether an embedding manages to suppress relighting effects while retaining defect-relevant texture information is an empirical question. Calling it relighting-invariant states the intended property, not a measured trade-off.
Likewise, could equivariance preserve a structural defect rather than normalizing it away?

That is the intended distinction: predictable behavior under registration changes need not mean discarding structural information. The embedding is meant to represent structure in a way that remains meaningful when registration changes. But the proposal alone does not prove that novel structural defects remain detectable, particularly under unseen camera shifts.
So there are two different kinds of uncertainty here: whether the embeddings behave as intended and whether the thresholds deliver the numerical targets?

Yes. Learning the intended structural and texture properties is one question. Achieving ≥90% defect recall at ≤5% image-level false-positive rate under unseen benign shifts, separately for structural and texture defects, is another. The separate 95th-percentile thresholds specify part of ShiftGuard’s proposed decision setup, but neither the embedding descriptions nor those percentiles are results.
Can we state ShiftGuard succinctly without adding a particular architecture or claiming it works already?

ShiftGuard is a proposed visual anomaly-detection approach that learns registration-equivariant structural embeddings and relighting-invariant texture embeddings from augmented normal images, with separate 95th-percentile image-level thresholds. It is intended to distinguish novel manufacturing defects from unseen benign illumination and camera shifts using only defect-free training images and no anomalous calibration data. Whether it meets the ≥90% recall and ≤5% image-level false-positive-rate targets for structural and texture defects separately is not established by the proposal.
Will ShiftGuard’s relighting invariance suppress faint texture defects that resemble localized illumination changes?

It could, but the proposal does not establish that it will. If the texture embedding treats a faint defect and a localized illumination change as equivalent, the defect may become difficult to distinguish from benign variation. Relighting invariance is intended to reduce responses to lighting changes; whether it also reduces responses to defect-relevant texture changes is the concern in your question.
So the same property that helps with benign shifts might hurt texture-defect recall?

Yes, that is the potential trade-off. Stability under relighting is useful only if the representation remains sensitive to actual texture defects. For faint defects that resemble localized lighting changes, those two aims may be hard to separate. The proposal alone does not tell us where ShiftGuard draws that boundary.
Does calling the embedding “relighting-invariant” imply that it ignores any localized change in brightness?

No. The phrase states an intended behavior under relighting; it does not define exactly which changes the embedding treats as relighting, or whether its invariance extends to every localized brightness change. Nor does it specify how much texture information is retained. We cannot infer from the name alone that all faint, localized defects would be suppressed.
But if a defect looks like illumination to a person, wouldn't the embedding have the same problem?

A resemblance raises the concern, but it does not settle what the embedding represents. Two changes that look similar in one respect need not be identical in every feature the embedding could retain. Conversely, if the embedding does map them similarly, its texture score may have little basis for separating them. Which case applies to ShiftGuard is not specified.
Can the separate 95th-percentile texture threshold fix that if the embedding has already suppressed the defect?

A threshold cannot recover a distinction that is absent from the score it receives. If a faint defect produces essentially the same image-level texture score as benign relighting, changing the threshold alone cannot reliably distinguish the two. That is a conditional limitation, not a finding that ShiftGuard’s embedding actually collapses those cases.
Could setting the threshold lower still catch some of the faint defects?

Possibly, if their scores remain distinguishable enough to cross a lower threshold. But a lower threshold could also flag more benign images. The question is not simply whether sensitivity can be increased; it is whether faint texture defects can remain distinguishable while benign illumination changes are not mistaken for defects.
Is this risk specifically about faint texture defects, rather than every texture defect?

Your question singles out faint texture defects that resemble localized illumination changes. It does not imply that all texture defects resemble lighting changes or that all would be affected equally. The concern is strongest conceptually where a defect-relevant signal overlaps with the kind of variation the embedding is meant to discount.
Does learning the embedding only from augmented normal images resolve the ambiguity?

Not by itself. Learning from augmented normal images is part of ShiftGuard’s proposal, but that description does not show how its representation treats faint, unseen texture defects. Without defect examples in training or anomalous calibration, the intended relighting invariance and the required sensitivity to novel defects must coexist without using those examples to draw the distinction directly.
Would it be fair to say the approach assumes localized illumination changes and faint defects are distinguishable?

I would phrase that more cautiously. ShiftGuard aims to retain defect-relevant texture information while being insensitive to relighting. Your question identifies a case in which those aims could conflict. The proposal does not state that the two kinds of change are always distinguishable, and it does not establish that the learned embedding separates them in this case.
What would a failure look like in terms of the original requirement?

If faint texture defects were suppressed enough to go unflagged, that could reduce texture-defect recall, including under the unseen benign shifts covered by the goal. The requirement is at least 90% defect recall at no more than a 5% image-level false-positive rate for texture defects separately. This is a possible failure mode to consider, not a claim that ShiftGuard misses that target.
So I shouldn't answer the question with a definite yes or a definite no yet?

Right. The defensible answer is that relighting invariance might suppress faint texture defects when their distinguishing signal resembles a localized illumination change. It might also preserve enough texture information to detect them. The stated proposal does not determine which happens, so the risk remains an open question rather than an established outcome.

Let me make the concern more precise: under unseen spatially varying relighting, ShiftGuard’s texture branch will recall less than 90% of faint stain defects at a 5% image-level false-positive rate. Is that a fair hypothesis?

Yes. That is a specific, untested prediction about ShiftGuard’s texture branch. It says that, when operating at a 5% image-level false-positive rate under unseen spatially varying relighting, the branch will detect fewer than 90% of faint stain defects. It does not say that this outcome has been observed.
Why specify spatially varying relighting rather than relighting in general?

It narrows the condition you are concerned about: illumination changes that vary across the image, rather than describing every kind of relighting. That matters to the hypothesis because a locally changing appearance could resemble a faint stain. The prediction is limited to unseen spatially varying relighting; it is not a prediction about all illumination changes.
Am I claiming that a faint stain and a lighting change are visually identical?

No. The hypothesis does not require them to be identical. It raises the possibility that ShiftGuard’s intended relighting invariance reduces the texture branch’s sensitivity to some faint stain signals under that condition. Whether that happens is precisely what remains uncertain.
What does “faint” contribute to the statement?

It identifies the subset of stain defects at issue. The prediction is not that the texture branch will miss every stain or every texture defect. It is specifically about recall for faint stain defects, whose detectable appearance may be harder to preserve while discounting relighting.
And why call out the texture branch instead of ShiftGuard as a whole?

The hypothesis concerns the branch intended to represent texture while remaining invariant to relighting. Naming that branch prevents the claim from being read as a prediction about ShiftGuard’s structural branch or every possible way its outputs might be used. No whole-system result is stated here.
Does “at a 5% image-level FPR” mean 5% of the faint stains are missed?

No. The 5% figure is the image-level false-positive rate: the proportion of defect-free images flagged at that operating point. Recall concerns the faint stain defects. “Less than 90% recall” means fewer than 90% of those defects are detected under the stated condition; it is a separate quantity from the 5% false-positive rate.
Could I phrase the prediction as ‘recall is at most 90%’?
That would change its boundary. The hypothesis says recall is strictly less than 90%, not at most 90%. A recall of exactly 90% would not satisfy the prediction as written.
Does the hypothesis say what happens if I allow a higher false-positive rate?

No. It predicts recall at the specified 5% image-level false-positive rate. It does not state the recall at a higher or lower false-positive rate, nor does it assert that no operating point could improve detection of faint stains.
The proposal has separate 95th-percentile image-level thresholds. Does that automatically put the texture branch at the 5% FPR in this hypothesis?

No. A 95th-percentile threshold refers to the scores used for calibration. The false-positive rate under unseen spatially varying relighting would still have to be determined; it does not automatically equal 5%. The hypothesis specifies a 5% image-level FPR operating point and predicts what faint-stain recall would be there.
So is this hypothesis about the threshold choice, or about the representation?

It states a predicted outcome for the texture branch at a specified operating point, without assigning a proven cause. Relighting invariance motivates the concern about faint stains, but the statement does not establish whether any shortfall would come from the embedding, thresholding, or their interaction.
Would less than 90% faint-stain recall at that operating point conflict with the intended texture-defect target?

It would identify a shortfall for faint stain defects relative to a 90% recall benchmark at 5% image-level FPR. The broader goal calls for at least 90% recall at no more than 5% image-level FPR for texture defects under unseen benign shifts. The hypothesis does not, by itself, establish the measured result for texture defects as a whole.
Can we say the hypothesis predicts all texture defects will fall below 90% recall?
No. It names faint stain defects specifically. Extending the prediction to other texture defects would go beyond its scope, even though stains fall within the texture-related concern.
Does it say anything about structural defects or unseen camera shifts?

No. Neither structural-defect recall nor performance under unseen camera shifts is predicted here. The condition is unseen spatially varying relighting, the subject is faint stain defects, and the output in question is ShiftGuard’s texture branch.
Should the word ‘will’ make us treat this as a confident result?

No. ‘Will’ expresses the outcome being hypothesized, not evidence that it has happened. Without an observed evaluation in the stated condition, the claim remains a prediction that could be supported or contradicted.
Could the opposite happen—could the texture branch retain faint stains despite being relighting-invariant?

Yes, that is logically possible. Relighting invariance need not erase every localized texture difference. If ShiftGuard retains the information that distinguishes faint stains from benign spatially varying relighting, the predicted below-90% recall need not occur. The hypothesis leaves that question open to evidence.

Then the concise version is: at a 5% image-level false-positive rate under unseen spatially varying relighting, ShiftGuard’s texture branch is predicted to detect fewer than 90% of faint stain defects?
Exactly. That preserves the operating point, the unseen relighting condition, the specific defect subset, and the strict below-90% recall prediction, without presenting it as a measured result.

Let’s make the evaluation concrete: train ShiftGuard on normal MVTec AD images, then measure faint-stain and scratch recall under held-out spatial relighting at a normal-only 5% image-level false-positive rate.

That is a plan, not a result. Normal MVTec AD images provide the training input. The evaluation would measure recall separately for faint stains and scratches under held-out spatial relighting, at an image-level false-positive-rate operating point established using normal images only. It directly probes whether defects remain detectable when the appearance changes because of spatial relighting.
What does “normal MVTec AD” restrict in the training step?

It restricts training to defect-free MVTec AD images. The plan does not call for training ShiftGuard on stain or scratch examples. Those defect types appear in what you intend to measure, not in the stated training input.
And “normal-only 5% FPR” is a restriction on how the operating point is chosen?

Yes. The 5% figure refers to the image-level false-positive rate, and “normal-only” rules out using anomalous examples to choose that operating point. It does not mean that only normal images are involved in measuring recall: recall for faint stains and scratches necessarily concerns defective examples.
Would measuring recall on defective images violate the no-anomalous-calibration condition?

No. Using defective examples to evaluate recall is different from using them to train ShiftGuard or calibrate its decision setting. The plan keeps calibration normal-only while measuring how often faint stains and scratches are detected.
Does the plan say to combine stains and scratches into one recall number?

No. It says to measure faint-stain and scratch recall. Keeping those measurements distinguishable matters: an aggregate could hide poor recall for one of the two. The plan does not specify any additional way of combining their results.
Why include scratches if the concern is about relighting suppressing faint stains?

The faint-stain measurement addresses that concern directly. Scratch recall adds another named defect type to measure under the same held-out spatial-relighting condition and normal-only 5% FPR operating point. The plan does not state what scratch recall will be or assign scratches a particular role in explaining any result.
Should I call the scratches the structural control?

That would add a designation the plan does not give them. You can say the plan measures scratch recall as well as faint-stain recall, but it does not explicitly define scratches as a control or say that the scratch measurement, by itself, establishes structural-defect performance.
What is held out about the spatial relighting?

The wording says the spatial relighting used for the measurement is held out. It does not describe the relighting patterns, how they are produced, or the exact split used to hold them out. The important stated condition is that recall is measured under spatial relighting not used as part of the training condition being evaluated.
Is that the same as testing every unseen illumination shift?

No. Held-out spatial relighting gives the plan a specific unseen-shift condition to assess. It does not imply coverage of every illumination change, and it says nothing about performance under every possible camera shift.
Could I simply use ShiftGuard’s separate 95th-percentile thresholds and report that the FPR is 5%?

A 95th-percentile calibration threshold has a nominal upper-tail interpretation for the scores used to set it. That alone does not establish a 5% image-level false-positive rate under held-out spatial relighting. The plan calls for measurement at a normal-only 5% FPR operating point; the wording does not specify exactly how that point is obtained or how ShiftGuard’s separate threshold outputs are handled.
So the 5% is an operating condition, not a predicted recall?
Correct. The 5% is the image-level false-positive-rate condition. Faint-stain recall and scratch recall are the quantities to measure at that condition. The plan supplies no measured recall values.
Does the plan already say faint-stain recall will be below 90%?

No. It calls for measuring faint-stain recall under the stated conditions; it does not report whether the result is below, equal to, or above 90%. The measurement would inform the concern about sensitivity to faint stains, rather than presupposing an answer.
If the measured faint-stain recall were low, would this plan alone tell us why?

Not necessarily. A recall measurement would characterize performance at the specified operating point under held-out spatial relighting. By itself, it would not establish whether any shortfall arose from the texture embedding’s relighting invariance, the image-level decision setting, or another aspect of ShiftGuard. The plan does not include a causal attribution procedure.
Likewise, good scratch recall wouldn’t automatically explain what happened with stains?

Right. The two recall measurements can be compared descriptively, but one does not, on its own, explain the other. The plan asks how each defect type fares under the same stated condition; it does not prescribe an explanation for any difference.
What exactly makes the false-positive rate image-level here?

An image-level false positive is a normal image flagged as defective. At a 5% image-level FPR, the rate concerns normal images, not the number of individual suspicious regions within them. The plan does not specify how an image-level score or alert is formed.
Does “normal-only” mean the held-out relighting must also be applied only to normal images?

No. “Normal-only” qualifies the false-positive-rate operating point, not the entire evaluation. The plan also calls for measuring defect recall under held-out spatial relighting. It does not specify the precise image-processing or data-construction steps used to create that condition.
Are faint stains and scratches guaranteed to be equally represented in this measurement?

The plan does not state their counts, proportions, or selection criteria. It names both recall measurements, but it does not justify assuming that the two defect groups have the same size or composition.
Can we say this test settles the broader target for structural and texture defects?

Not from the plan alone. It specifies measurements for faint stains and scratches under held-out spatial relighting at normal-only 5% image-level FPR. The broader target concerns structural and texture defects separately under unseen benign shifts. These planned measurements are relevant, but no outcomes—or full coverage of that broader target—are stated.
How would you phrase the plan without smuggling in an expected result?

Train ShiftGuard using normal MVTec AD images. At a normal-only 5% image-level false-positive-rate operating point, measure faint-stain recall and scratch recall under held-out spatial relighting. That wording preserves the training restriction, the two measurements, the shift condition, and the operating point without asserting what either recall will be.
For the evaluation activity, train ShiftGuard on defect-free MVTec AD images and score held-out faint stains and scratches under unseen spatial relighting at a normal-calibrated 5% image-level FPR.

That specifies the activity without stating an outcome. ShiftGuard is trained on defect-free MVTec AD images; held-out faint-stain and scratch examples are then scored under unseen spatial relighting. The 5% image-level false-positive-rate operating point is calibrated using normal images, not anomalous examples. The resulting scores can be used to assess detection, but no scores or recall values are supplied here.
Does “held-out” apply to the defect examples, the spatial relighting, or both?

In this wording, faint stains and scratches are held out, and the spatial relighting is unseen. Those are distinct constraints: the defect examples are not part of the stated training input, and the relighting condition is not one the activity treats as already seen. The wording does not specify a split procedure.
What do you mean by scoring rather than reporting recall?

Scoring names what ShiftGuard does to the held-out examples under the relighting condition. Recall would be a performance quantity derived from whether defect examples are detected at the operating point. This activity states that the examples are scored; it does not give their scores or the resulting faint-stain or scratch recall.
Does the 5% FPR mean five percent of the stains are allowed to be missed?

No. False-positive rate concerns defect-free images incorrectly flagged at the image level. Missed stains or scratches affect defect recall, which is a different quantity. The activity identifies a normal-calibrated 5% image-level FPR operating point for scoring the held-out defects.
Can we say the false-positive rate will necessarily remain 5% under the unseen spatial relighting?

No. “Normal-calibrated 5% FPR” describes the calibration basis and operating point. It does not, by itself, guarantee that the measured image-level false-positive rate under unseen spatial relighting is exactly 5%. That condition could affect normal images’ scores, and no measured false-positive rate under it is provided.
Is anomalous data used to choose that operating point?

Not as stated. The operating point is normal-calibrated, and training uses defect-free MVTec AD images. The held-out faint stains and scratches are subjects of scoring, not examples specified for training or calibration.
Does this activity target the question about faint stains looking like localized lighting changes?

Yes. Scoring held-out faint stains under unseen spatial relighting is directly relevant to whether ShiftGuard remains sensitive to them when lighting varies across an image. Scratch scores provide a second named defect measurement under that condition. The activity does not yet answer whether relighting invariance suppresses the faint stains.
Is it accurate to say this activity tests the prediction of less than 90% faint-stain recall?

It can provide evidence relevant to that prediction: the held-out faint stains are scored under unseen spatial relighting at the specified normal-calibrated operating point. But the activity does not report faint-stain recall, and normal calibration alone does not establish that the observed FPR under the unseen condition is exactly 5%. Those distinctions matter when comparing any eventual measurement with a prediction stated at 5% image-level FPR.
Should I attribute the faint-stain scores specifically to ShiftGuard’s texture branch?

The activity says to score the examples with ShiftGuard; it does not explicitly identify which branch’s scores are recorded. ShiftGuard’s texture branch is central to the faint-stain concern, but describing a branch-specific measurement here would add a detail that this activity does not state.
And I should not call scratches a structural control unless that is specified?

Correct. The activity names held-out scratches as another set of defects to score, but it does not designate them as a control or assign them a branch. Their scores should not be given an unstated role.
What can we conclude once the activity is described, before seeing any scores?

Only what will be done: defect-free MVTec AD training, followed by scoring held-out faint stains and scratches under unseen spatial relighting at a normal-calibrated 5% image-level FPR operating point. The description alone does not establish recall, performance under the relighting, or whether the faint-stain hypothesis holds.

The MVTec AD result is in: under unseen spatial relighting, ShiftGuard recalled 76% of faint stains versus 92% of scratches at a 5% image-level false-positive rate. How should we describe that finding?

Report the two measurements together with their condition and operating point: on MVTec AD, under unseen spatial relighting, ShiftGuard’s faint-stain recall was 76% and its scratch recall was 92%, at a 5% image-level false-positive rate. Scratch recall was 16 percentage points higher than faint-stain recall in that evaluation.
Is the difference 16%, or 16 percentage points?
Sixteen percentage points. Subtracting the reported recall rates gives 92% minus 76% = 16 percentage points. Calling it a 16% relative difference would be a different calculation.
